title: Designing for Change: Extension Points and Configuration
summary: Deciding where a design should flex for future requirements versus where flexibility is premature and costly.

slides.markdown:
Every design decision about flexibility is a bet: build an extension point now and you pay complexity today for change that might never come; skip it and a real future requirement costs a rewrite instead of a plug-in. Neither instinct — "make everything configurable" or "just hard-code it" — is right by default.

Think of it like leaving a doorway in a wall versus knocking one through later: cheap if you know traffic is coming through that spot, wasted framing if it never gets used.

This topic covers where a real extension point pays for itself, when configuration beats a new class, and how to tell a documented near-term need from a guess dressed up as one.

slides.sectionTitle: Extension points: a seam where new behavior plugs in without touching existing code
slides.markdown:
An **extension point** is a seam in your design where new behavior can be plugged in without touching the code that's already working — a strategy interface, a plugin registry, a hook callback. It's the mechanical version of the **open/closed principle**: open for extension, closed for modification.

The test for whether a spot deserves an extension point isn't "could this vary someday" — almost anything could. It's whether you can point at a second, concrete case today, or a documented near-term one, that needs to plug in differently. A payment flow that already needs to support both Stripe and a bank transfer has earned a `PaymentProvider` interface; a payment flow that only ever processes Stripe hasn't.

Extension points are seams you add where the variation is real, not insurance against every hypothetical.

slides.sectionTitle: Configuration vs code: when a behavior should be a config value instead of a new class
slides.markdown:
Not every behavior difference needs a new class. **Configuration** — a value read at startup or runtime, like a feature flag, a threshold, or a connection string — fits when the *logic* stays the same and only a *parameter* changes. **Code** — a new class, strategy, or branch — fits when the actual behavior or algorithm differs, not just a number.

| | Configuration | Code |
|---|---|---|
| Fits when | Same logic, different value (timeout, limit, on/off) | Different logic or algorithm entirely |
| Change cost | Edit a value, often no redeploy | Write, test, and ship new code |
| Risk of overuse | A config file that's really an untested programming language | A new class for every value that should've been a setting |

**How to decide:** ask whether the difference is "how much/whether" (configuration) or "how" (code). A retry count is configuration; a completely different retry strategy — exponential backoff vs a fixed queue — is code.

slides.markdown:
<<< Image: a checkout flow with a single highlighted seam point labelled PaymentStrategy interface; three concrete implementations — StripeStrategy, BankTransferStrategy, WalletStrategy — plug into that one seam; the rest of the checkout flow has no seams or branches drawn >>>

The checkout flow needs exactly one seam: how payment is actually processed, since that's the one thing that genuinely varies today across Stripe, bank transfer, and wallet balance. A `PaymentStrategy` interface sits at that single point; everything else in checkout — validating the cart, applying discounts, sending a receipt — has no seam because none of it varies yet.

The discipline is restraint: one seam where the real variation lives, not a seam at every step just because some step theoretically could change.

slides.sectionTitle: Premature abstraction: the cost of an extension point nobody uses yet
slides.markdown:
An extension point nobody uses yet isn't neutral — it has a real, ongoing cost. Every interface, every plugin registry, every layer of indirection you add makes the code harder to read (you now trace through the abstraction to find what actually runs) and harder to change (the abstraction itself is one more thing a future refactor has to account for).

A `PaymentStrategy` interface built for a single Stripe implementation gives you all the indirection of polymorphism and none of the benefit — every call still resolves to the same one class, forever, until a second implementation shows up, if it ever does.

The cost of premature abstraction is paid daily, by everyone reading the code; the cost of skipping it is paid once, later, only if the variation actually materializes.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: building a "flexible" framework for a single known use case
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll build this as a generic, pluggable framework now — that way it's ready for whatever we need later."

**Why it's wrong:** a framework built for imagined future cases, with exactly one real caller, optimizes for requirements nobody has confirmed yet. It's usually wrong about *how* the future need will actually look — the plugin points end up in the wrong places, and when a real second use case finally shows up, it often doesn't fit the guessed-at extension seams anyway, forcing a rework regardless.

**Correct model:** build the concrete solution for the case you actually have. Extract the abstraction when a second real case arrives — you'll have two real examples to generalize from instead of one guess, and the resulting seam will fit the actual variation instead of an imagined one.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a feature-flagged behavior swap vs a hard-coded conditional
Telling speculative flexibility apart from a documented near-term need
slides.markdown:
The honest question before adding flexibility isn't "might we need this?" — almost anything might. It's "is there a ticket, a roadmap item, or a stated requirement for this, or am I guessing?" A payment flow with a signed contract to add a second provider next quarter has a documented near-term need; a payment flow where "we might add crypto someday" is speculation, however plausible it sounds.

This is the same discipline behind **YAGNI** ("you aren't gonna need it") — build for the requirement you actually have, not the one you're imagining. Speculative flexibility dressed up as foresight is still speculation, and it's paid for by everyone maintaining the code in the meantime.

When you catch yourself justifying an abstraction with "just in case," that's usually the signal to build the concrete version instead and wait for a real second case.
